An intersection element fixes the new point and preserves the old orbit. Matching its complementary restriction by an element of P leaves an actual Q element supported on X; the stated kernel containment is both necessary and sufficient.

Prefix induction uses the two old/new end groups and Lemma2; necessity uses actual C submarkings. The first test is trivial. For a pure first transposition, the preceding prefix contains the full symmetric group on its root orbit.

Each supported saturation is a direct product. The two root sets have intersection X0 union Y0 union {c}; the remaining two restriction images are those of L0 and T0. Nestedness and disjoint original sides are essential.

Projection is injective on the untwisted end, so its intersection with the twisted end is the actual middle subgroup. This proves only the valid forward twist and invokes the attributed standard end criterion.

The two original lists satisfy root-fixing from the string relations and separated supports. Conjugation by u identifies the right attachment. Intervals ending at v use a pure attachment followed by a disjoint endpoint twist. For intervals crossing both marks, (uv)^3=beta makes the rectangle lemma applicable. Necessity follows by submarkings, reversal and conjugation.

A pure split supplies the left extension by point renaming and the right by Corollary4. In the impure parity graph, successive supported kernels are the same alternating subgroup. The old S7 counterexample fails exactly at Sym3 versus Alt3.
